claim: Many insects use patterns of polarized light in the sky to orient and navigate.
source: Many insects use patterns of polarized light in the sky to orient and navigate.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of insect navigation, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Neurons tuned to the angle of polarization of ultraviolet light are found throughout the anterior visual pathway in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Neurons tuned to the angle of polarization of ultraviolet light are found throughout the anterior visual pathway, connecting the optic lobes with the central complex via the anterior optic tubercle and bulb, in a homologous organization to the 'sky compass' pathways described in other insects.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing polarization-tuned neurons in multiple regions of the anterior visual pathway.

claim: The anterior visual pathway in Drosophila connects the optic lobes with the central complex via the anterior optic tubercle and bulb.
source: Neurons tuned to the angle of polarization of ultraviolet light are found throughout the anterior visual pathway, connecting the optic lobes with the central complex via the anterior optic tubercle and bulb, in a homologous organization to the 'sky compass' pathways described in other insects.
evidence: This anatomical connectivity is demonstrated through the tracing experiments and imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The organization of the anterior visual pathway in Drosophila is homologous to the 'sky compass' pathways described in other insects.
source: Neurons tuned to the angle of polarization of ultraviolet light are found throughout the anterior visual pathway, connecting the optic lobes with the central complex via the anterior optic tubercle and bulb, in a homologous organization to the 'sky compass' pathways described in other insects.
evidence: This claim is based on comparative analysis with known sky compass pathways in other insects, supported by anatomical and functional similarities.

claim: A consistent, map-like organization of neural tunings in the peripheral visual system is transformed into a reduced representation suited to flexible processing in the central brain.
source: We detail how a consistent, map-like organization of neural tunings in the peripheral visual system is transformed into a reduced representation suited to flexible processing in the central brain.
evidence: This transformation is demonstrated through the functional imaging data showing polarotopic organization in peripheral regions and more flexible encoding in central regions.

claim: The central complex in Dipteran flies is believed to coordinate spatial memory, object memory, and action selection behaviors.
source: In Dipteran flies, as in other invertebrates, a collection of neuropils known as the central complex (CX) is believed to coordinate such behaviors and plays a role in spatial memory, object memory, and action selection (Giraldo et al., 2018; Neuser et al., 2008; Ofstad et al., 2011; Strausfeld and Hirth, 2013), in addition to homeostatic processes including hunger and sleep (Donlea et al., 2014; Dus et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on central complex function.

claim: The central complex plays a role in homeostatic processes including hunger and sleep.
source: In Dipteran flies, as in other invertebrates, a collection of neuropils known as the central complex (CX) is believed to coordinate such behaviors and plays a role in spatial memory, object memory, and action selection (Giraldo et al., 2018; Neuser et al., 2008; Ofstad et al., 2011; Strausfeld and Hirth, 2013), in addition to homeostatic processes including hunger and sleep (Donlea et al., 2014; Dus et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on central complex function in homeostatic processes.

claim: Activity in a network of central complex neurons in Drosophila encodes and maintains a representation of the animal's angular heading relative to its environment.
source: Recent studies in Drosophila have revealed that activity in a network of CX neurons encodes and maintains a representation of the animal's angular heading relative to its environment (Kim et al., 2017; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015), with similarity to head-direction cells in vertebrates (Taube et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies demonstrating heading representation in the central complex.

claim: The neural representation of heading in Drosophila central complex is similar to head-direction cells in vertebrates.
source: Recent studies in Drosophila have revealed that activity in a network of CX neurons encodes and maintains a representation of the animal's angular heading relative to its environment (Kim et al., 2017; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015), with similarity to head-direction cells in vertebrates (Taube et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim draws a comparison between Drosophila and vertebrate systems based on cited research.

claim: The neural representation of heading in Drosophila can be updated by internal, proprioceptive estimates of self-motion during locomotion.
source: This neural representation of heading can be updated by internal, proprioceptive estimates of self-motion during locomotion, and by external cues, such as moving visual patterns and directional airflow (Fisher et al., 2019; Green et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019; Okubo et al., 2020; Shiozaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research on heading representation updates.

claim: The neural representation of heading in Drosophila can be updated by external cues such as moving visual patterns and directional airflow.
source: This neural representation of heading can be updated by internal, proprioceptive estimates of self-motion during locomotion, and by external cues, such as moving visual patterns and directional airflow (Fisher et al., 2019; Green et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019; Okubo et al., 2020; Shiozaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research on sensory inputs to the heading system.

claim: In locusts, crickets, bees, butterflies, and beetles, the functional organization of the central complex has been studied in the context of navigation via celestial cues, particularly polarized light.
source: In other insects, including locusts, crickets, bees, butterflies, and beetles, the functional organization of the CX has frequently been studied in the context of navigation via celestial cues, particularly polarized light (Heinze, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review on central complex function in insect navigation.

claim: The pattern of polarization in the sky is formed by scattering of light in the atmosphere.
source: The nearly ever-present pattern of polarization in the sky, formed by scattering of light in the atmosphere, offers an indicator of orientation to organisms able to detect and interpret it, and may be more stable than terrestrial landmarks (Cronin and Marshall, 2011; Dacke et al., 2003; Horváth and Varju, 2004; Mappes and Homberg, 2004; Frisch, 1949; Wehner and Müller, 2006).
evidence: This is a well-established physical phenomenon supported by multiple citations.

claim: Skylight polarization patterns may be more stable than terrestrial landmarks for navigation.
source: The nearly ever-present pattern of polarization in the sky, formed by scattering of light in the atmosphere, offers an indicator of orientation to organisms able to detect and interpret it, and may be more stable than terrestrial landmarks (Cronin and Marshall, 2011; Dacke et al., 2003; Horváth and Varju, 2004; Mappes and Homberg, 2004; Frisch, 1949; Wehner and Müller, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on polarization-based navigation.

claim: In non-Dipteran insects, a multimodal neural circuit transmits polarization signals from the eyes to the central complex.
source: In these non-Dipteran insects, a multimodal neural circuit transmits polarization signals from the eyes to the central complex (el Jundi et al., 2015; el Jundi et al., 2014; Heinze, 2013; Heinze and Reppert, 2011; Homberg et al., 2011; Pfeiffer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research on insect polarization pathways.

claim: The sky compass pathway in non-Dipteran insects is proposed to process skylight polarization patterns and information about the position of the sun to provide an animal with a sense of direction.
source: This circuit is known as the 'sky compass' pathway for its proposed role in processing skylight polarization patterns and information about the position of the sun to bestow an animal with a sense of direction.
evidence: This claim describes the proposed function of the sky compass pathway based on research in other insects.

claim: The anterior visual pathway in Drosophila has been postulated to represent the homologue of the sky compass pathway.
source: In Drosophila, the anterior visual pathway (AVP), which comprises neurons connecting the medulla, anterior optic tubercle, bulb, and ellipsoid body, has been postulated to represent the homologue of the sky compass pathway (Omoto et al., 2017; Timaeus et al., 2020; Warren et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research proposing this homology.

claim: Visual processing in the anterior visual pathway appears to be segregated into three topographically organized, parallel streams.
source: Visual processing in the AVP appears to be segregated into three topographically organized, parallel streams, of which two have been shown to encode distinct small-field, unpolarized stimuli (Omoto et al., 2017; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2013; Shiozaki and Kazama, 2017; Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on anterior visual pathway organization.

claim: Two of the three parallel streams in the anterior visual pathway have been shown to encode distinct small-field, unpolarized stimuli.
source: Visual processing in the AVP appears to be segregated into three topographically organized, parallel streams, of which two have been shown to encode distinct small-field, unpolarized stimuli (Omoto et al., 2017; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2013; Shiozaki and Kazama, 2017; Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on visual encoding in the anterior visual pathway.

claim: The neurons involved in polarization processing in Drosophila have not been identified beyond peripheral circuits of the dorsal rim area prior to this study.
source: The neurons involved in polarization processing in Drosophila have not been identified beyond peripheral circuits of the dorsal rim area, a specialized region of the eye for detecting skylight polarization (Fortini and Rubin, 1991; Wada, 1974; Weir et al., 2016; Weir and Dickinson, 2015; Wernet et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim establishes the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses, supported by citations to previous work on the dorsal rim area.

claim: The dorsal rim area is a specialized region of the eye for detecting skylight polarization.
source: The neurons involved in polarization processing in Drosophila have not been identified beyond peripheral circuits of the dorsal rim area, a specialized region of the eye for detecting skylight polarization (Fortini and Rubin, 1991; Wada, 1974; Weir et al., 2016; Weir and Dickinson, 2015; Wernet et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 1980).
evidence: This is an established fact about the dorsal rim area supported by multiple citations.

claim: Behavioral experiments have demonstrated that Drosophila orient relative to polarization patterns while walking and in tethered-flight.
source: Behavioral experiments have demonstrated that Drosophila orient relative to polarization patterns while walking and in tethered-flight (Mathejczyk and Wernet, 2019; Stephens et al., 1953; Warren et al., 2018; Weir and Dickinson, 2012; Wernet et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Within the dorsal rim area, each R7/R8 pair is sensitive to a different angle of polarization, organized in a 'polarotopic' fashion.
source: Within a narrow strip of skyward-facing ommatidia in each eye, known as the dorsal rim area (DRA), each R7/R8 pair is sensitive to a different angle of polarization (AoP, also referred to as the e-vector orientation), organized in a 'polarotopic' fashion (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the schematic in Figure 1A and established knowledge about the dorsal rim area.

claim: The dorsal rim area photoreceptors cover the complete 180° range of polarization orientations.
source: This specialized array of polarization detectors covers the complete 180° range of orientations and, with a peak spectral sensitivity to UV light, is well-suited to sensing the patterns of polarized light in the sky (Feiler et al., 1992; Salcedo et al., 1999; Sharkey et al., 2020; Weir et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on dorsal rim area photoreceptors.

claim: Dorsal rim area photoreceptors have a peak spectral sensitivity to UV light.
source: This specialized array of polarization detectors covers the complete 180° range of orientations and, with a peak spectral sensitivity to UV light, is well-suited to sensing the patterns of polarized light in the sky (Feiler et al., 1992; Salcedo et al., 1999; Sharkey et al., 2020; Weir et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on photoreceptor spectral sensitivity.

claim: DmDRA1 neurons span approximately 10 MEDRA columns.
source: Individual DmDRA1 neurons span approximately 10 MEDRA columns and receive input exclusively from DRA R7 photoreceptors while avoiding input from non-DRA columns (Sancer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical characterization.

claim: DmDRA1 neurons receive input exclusively from DRA R7 photoreceptors while avoiding input from non-DRA columns.
source: Individual DmDRA1 neurons span approximately 10 MEDRA columns and receive input exclusively from DRA R7 photoreceptors while avoiding input from non-DRA columns (Sancer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical characterization.

claim: DmDRA2 neurons receive exclusive input from DRA R8 photoreceptors.
source: DmDRA2 receives exclusive input from DRA R8 photoreceptors.
evidence: This claim is based on the anatomical characterization cited in the manuscript.

claim: Both DmDRA1 and DmDRA2 subtypes are thought likely to respond to polarized light due to their contact with polarization-sensitive photoreceptors.
source: Due to their contact with polarization-sensitive photoreceptors, both DmDRA subtypes are thought likely to respond to polarized light (Sancer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical connectivity, supported by a citation.

claim: The split-Gal4 driver R13E04-p65.AD, VT059781-Gal4.DBD is predominantly expressed in DmDRA1 neurons.
source: We found highly overlapping expression between these drivers (Figure 1B'), indicating that the split-Gal4 is predominantly expressed in DmDRA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-labeling experiment shown in Figure 1B'.

claim: DmDRA1 neurons are in close proximity to the proximal tip of each DRA R7/R8 pair.
source: We confirmed that DmDRA neurons in the split-Gal4 were also in close proximity to photoreceptor terminals in the MEDRA, and found clear overlap with the proximal tip of each DRA R7/R8 pair, providing further evidence of exclusive contact with DRA R7 (Figure 1B'').
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical imaging shown in Figure 1B''.

claim: The activity of DmDRA1 neurons varies with the angle of polarization presented.
source: We found that the activity of DmDRA1 neurons varied with the AoP presented and followed an approximately sinusoidal response profile typical of polarization-sensitive neurons (Heinze, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1C and the citation to typical polarization-sensitive neuron responses.

claim: DmDRA1 neurons follow an approximately sinusoidal response profile typical of polarization-sensitive neurons.
source: We found that the activity of DmDRA1 neurons varied with the AoP presented and followed an approximately sinusoidal response profile typical of polarization-sensitive neurons (Heinze, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the calcium imaging data and a citation to the characteristic response profile.

claim: DmDRA1 neurons have an average polarization-selectivity index (PSI) of 0.74.
source: Among DmDRA1 neurons, we found high PSI values throughout the population with an average of 0.74, while background regions in each recording contained an average PSI of 0.20 (Figure 1D,E, Appendix 1–table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: With the polarizer removed, PSI values in DmDRA1 neurons fell by approximately 80%.
source: With the polarizer removed, PSI values in DmDRA1 neurons fell by approximately 80% (Figure 1E,F), reflecting their lack of modulation and resulting in an average ΔPSI of 0.59, whereas PSI values in the background showed no change (Figure 1F), resulting in an average ΔPSI of 0.
evidence: This claim is supported by the control experiment data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Within the population of DmDRA1 neurons, the preferred angle of polarization shows a linear relationship with position, which is referred to as polarotopy.
source: Within the population of DmDRA1 neurons, we observed preferential responses to different angles of polarized light depending on their position in the MEDRA (Figure 1C,G). The preferred AoP showed a linear relationship with position, which we refer to as polarotopy (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial analysis of tuning data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: Moving anterior to posterior in the right optic lobe, the preferred angle of polarization in DmDRA1 neurons shifts counter-clockwise.
source: Moving anterior to posterior in the right optic lobe, the preferred AoP shifted counter-clockwise (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarotopy analysis shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: The polarotopy in the left optic lobe is mirrored compared to the right optic lobe, with a similar range of preferred angles of polarization represented in the opposite posterior-anterior direction.
source: This polarotopy was mirrored in the left optic lobe, with a similar range of preferred AoPs represented in the opposite posterior-anterior direction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The preferred angles of polarization of DmDRA1 neurons closely match those of R8 photoreceptors at similar positions.
source: Throughout the MEDRA, the preferred AoPs of DmDRA1 neurons closely matched those of R8 photoreceptors at similar positions (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of tuning data from DmDRA1 and R8 shown in the figures.

claim: R7/R8 photoreceptors are likely inhibitory.
source: Since R7/R8 are likely inhibitory (Davis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2008), we expected that the preferred AoP of a neuron postsynaptic to either R7 or R8 would be shifted by 90°.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on photoreceptor signaling.

claim: R7 signals are responsible for the predominant response characteristics of DmDRA1 neurons.
source: We therefore posit that it is R7 signals that are responsible for the predominant response characteristics of DmDRA1 neurons, consistent with the anatomical overlap between DmDRA1 and R7 terminals (Figure 1B'') and the established connectivity of the DmDRA1 subtype (Sancer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the tuning data, anatomical data, and cited connectivity information.

claim: DmDRA1 neurons show polarization opponency, with activity increases at preferred angles and inhibition at anti-preferred angles.
source: The preferred AoP of 0° caused an increase in activity relative to baseline, while flashes at 90° caused a decrease of greater magnitude, followed by a slight rebound above baseline after the offset of the flash (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flash response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: DmDRA1 neurons are inhibited by unpolarized light regardless of position in the MEDRA.
source: For light flashes with the polarizer removed we observed inhibition of DmDRA1 at all regions, regardless of position in the MEDRA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the control experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The excitation of DmDRA1 neurons by preferred angles of polarization is likely a release from R7-mediated inhibition.
source: This excitation is likely to be a release from R7-mediated inhibition, with R7 and DmDRA1 tuned to orthogonal angles of polarization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the response properties and known inhibitory nature of R7.

claim: In other insect species, polarization-sensitive photoreceptors in the dorsal rim are thought to provide input to transmedulla neurons.
source: In other insect species, polarization-sensitive photoreceptors in the dorsal rim are thought to provide input to transmedulla neurons (also referred to as line-tangential neurons), which project from the optic lobe to the anterior optic tubercle (AOTU) (el Jundi et al., 2011; Homberg et al., 2003; Immonen et al., 2017; Pfeiffer and Kinoshita, 2012; Zeller et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research in other insect species.

claim: In all insect species investigated, the small subunit of the AOTU is involved in processing polarized light signals.
source: In all species investigated, it is the small subunit of the AOTU (often called the lower-unit, LU) which is involved in processing polarized light signals (Heinze, 2013), although to our knowledge these signals have not been explored in transmedulla neurons themselves.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review and notes a gap in knowledge.

claim: Individual MeTu neurons typically innervate 10–15 columns of the medulla in layers M6–7.
source: The dendrites of individual MeTu neurons typically innervate 10–15 columns of the medulla in layers M6–7 (Omoto et al., 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and, as an ensemble, tile larger areas of the medulla (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical characterization and the figure.

claim: MeTu neurons as an ensemble tile larger areas of the medulla.
source: The dendrites of individual MeTu neurons typically innervate 10–15 columns of the medulla in layers M6–7 (Omoto et al., 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and, as an ensemble, tile larger areas of the medulla (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Trans-Tango labeling from DmDRA1-split identified a population of neurons in the dorsal medulla that project to the small, lateral subunit of the AOTU via the anterior optic tract.
source: We found that DmDRA1-split driving trans-Tango labeled a population of neurons in the dorsal medulla that project to the small, lateral subunit of the AOTU via a fiber bundle in the anterior optic tract (AOT) (Figure 2B), and matched the anatomy of MeTu neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the trans-Tango tracing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Trans-Tango labeling from Rh3/Rh4-Gal4 identified labeling of the small subunit of the AOTU.
source: We again found trans-Tango labeling of the small subunit of the AOTU (Figure 2C), indicating connectivity between UV-sensitive photoreceptors and MeTu neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the trans-Tango tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MeTu dendrites are in close proximity to DRA R7 terminals in layer M6 of the dorsal medulla.
source: Throughout layer M6 in the dorsal medulla, MeTu dendrites were in close proximity to non-DRA R7 terminals and at the dorsal-posterior margin we found clear overlap with DRA R7 terminals, distinguishable by their larger terminals and deeper projections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At least some MeTu neurons appear to receive input from DRA R7 photoreceptors.
source: In short, at least some MeTu neurons appear to receive input from DRA R7 photoreceptors (in addition to non-DRA photoreceptors and possibly DRA R8) and the putative connections revealed here suggest a parallel pathway for polarization signals in the MEDRA: DRA R7→DmDRA1, DmDRA1→MeTu, DRA R7→MeTu (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on the anatomical proximity data and trans-Tango results.

claim: There is a parallel pathway for polarization signals in the MEDRA: DRA R7→DmDRA1, DmDRA1→MeTu, DRA R7→MeTu.
source: In short, at least some MeTu neurons appear to receive input from DRA R7 photoreceptors (in addition to non-DRA photoreceptors and possibly DRA R8) and the putative connections revealed here suggest a parallel pathway for polarization signals in the MEDRA: DRA R7→DmDRA1, DmDRA1→MeTu, DRA R7→MeTu (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the connectivity data from trans-Tango and anatomical imaging.

claim: Both DmDRA1 and Rh3/Rh4 trans-Tango experiments predominantly labeled the intermediate-lateral domain (AOTUil) of the AOTU.
source: Both the DmDRA1 and Rh3/Rh4 trans-Tango experiments predominantly labeled the intermediate-lateral domain (AOTUil), with encroachment on the lateral domain (AOTUl) (Figure 2B''–C'').
evidence: This claim is supported by the trans-Tango labeling patterns shown in Figure 2B''–C''.

claim: No detectable intermediate-medial (AOTUim) or medial (AOTUm) labeling was found in either DmDRA1 or Rh3/Rh4 trans-Tango experiments.
source: We found no detectable intermediate-medial (AOTUim) or medial (AOTUm) labeling in either experiment (Figure 2B'–C').
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of labeling in these regions in the trans-Tango experiments.

claim: There is a consistent relationship between the anterior→posterior position of MeTu dendrites in the MEDRA and the ventral→dorsal position of MeTu axon terminals in the AOTU.
source: From confocal images of single-cell MCFO (MultiColor FlpOut) clones (Nern et al., 2015), we determined a consistent relationship between the anterior→posterior position of MeTu dendrites in the MEDRA and the ventral→dorsal position of MeTu axon terminals in the AOTU (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell clone data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: For MeTu neurons with dendrites outside of the MEDRA, there is no clear relationship between ventrodorsal position in the medulla and mediolateral position in the AOTU.
source: For MeTu neurons with dendrites outside of the MEDRA, we found no clear relationship between ventrodorsal position in the medulla and mediolateral position in the AOTU, confirming a previous study (Timaeus et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of single-cell clones and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Both R56F07 and R73C04 MeTu populations showed a statistically significant increase in average PSI values compared to controls with the polarizer removed.
source: Nonetheless, compared to control experiments with the polarizer removed, the polarizer caused a statistically significant increase in average PSI values among both MeTu populations (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The highest PSI values in R56F07 MeTu terminals were found within the most lateral regions of the population.
source: In R56F07, the most responsive MeTu terminals were found within the most lateral regions of the population (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial distribution of PSI values shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In R73C04 MeTu population, the most responsive terminals tended to be clustered in a narrow medial band.
source: In R73C04, the most responsive terminals tended to be clustered in a narrow medial band of the population (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), likely corresponding to the anterior region of AOTUil and possibly AOTUla.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial distribution of PSI values shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both R56F07 and R73C04 MeTu populations showed a predominant polarotopic organization with preferred angle of polarization shifting counter-clockwise from ventral to dorsal in the right AOTU.
source: Across animals, both populations showed a predominant polarotopic organization which matched our prediction: from ventral to dorsal in the right AOTU, the preferred AoP shifted counter-clockwise (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarotopy analysis shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Approximately 20% of MeTu experiments showed vertical organizations of responses that deviated from the predominant polarotopy.
source: However, we observed vertical organizations of responses which deviated from the norm in approximately 20% of experiments across both drivers.
evidence: This claim is based on the quantitative analysis of the polarotopy data across experiments.

claim: The most common deviation from predominant polarotopy resembled an inverted form with clockwise rotation of preferred angle of polarization from ventral to dorsal.
source: The most common of these resembled an inverted form of the predominant polarotopy (from ventral to dorsal in the right AOTU, the preferred AoP rotated clockwise) and also typically contained tunings to a different range of AoPs than the predominant organization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,E').
evidence: This claim is supported by the alternative polarotopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,E'.

claim: Distinct regions in the AOTU were modulated by either polarized or unpolarized light stimuli.
source: Distinct regions could be observed which were modulated by either the polarized or unpolarized light stimuli (green or blue, respectively, Figure 4A), along with areas that were equally active during both experiments (white, Figure 4A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined activity maps shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Lateral MeTu terminals in R73C04 showed a vertical polarotopic organization consistent with anatomical mapping.
source: Within ROIs drawn on lateral MeTu terminals in R73C04 (likely occupying the ventral AOTUlc domain, green ROIs, Figure 4A, left), we found moderate modulation of activity during the rotation of the polarizer (Figure 4B) which was sufficient to identify the preferred AoP. Like the terminals with above-threshold PSI values (Figure 3D), we observed a vertical polarotopic organization consistent with the anatomical mapping of MeTu neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D): from ventral to dorsal, the AoP rotated counter-clockwise in the right AOTU and clockwise in the left AOTU (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: An intermediate band of MeTu terminals showed clear responses to bars in ipsilateral-frontal and frontal positions.
source: Within an intermediate band of MeTu terminals (likely corresponding to AOTUla, blue ROIs, Figure 4A), left, we observed clear responses to bars in ipsilateral-frontal and frontal positions, with the more frontal position represented dorsally in the AOTU on both sides of the brain (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the bar response data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the ventral AOTU, responses to bars presented in the contralateral-lateral visual field (±90° azimuth) were found, outside the field of view of the ipsilateral eye.
source: In the ventral AOTU, we found responses to bars presented in the contralateral-lateral visual field (±90° azimuth), outside the field of view of the ipsilateral eye (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the bar response data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Retinotopic representations of both visual space and angles of polarization are found within different regions of the lateral and intermediate-lateral domains of the AOTU.
source: Together, these results suggest that retinotopic representations of both visual space and angles of polarization are found within different regions of the lateral and intermediate-lateral domains of the AOTU (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined polarization and bar response data.

claim: MeTu neurons were stimulated by a sparse dot-field pattern simulating forward thrust optic-flow.
source: Here, we found that MeTu neurons were indeed stimulated by a sparse dot-field pattern presented at different locations (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the optic-flow response data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Trans-Tango from R73C04-Gal4 MeTu neurons revealed clear labeling of a population of neurons projecting to the bulb resembling TuBu neurons.
source: We found clear labeling of a population of neurons projecting to the bulb which resembled the tubercular-bulbar (TuBu) neurons (Omoto et al., 2017; Figure 5A'), in addition to labeling of the inter-tubercle tract (ITT) (Strausfeld, 1976; Figure 5A''), suggesting inter-hemispheric signaling postsynaptic to MeTu neurons in the AOTU.
evidence: This claim is supported by the trans-Tango labeling shown in Figure 5A'.

claim: Trans-Tango from R73C04-Gal4 MeTu neurons revealed labeling of the inter-tubercle tract (ITT), suggesting inter-hemispheric signaling.
source: We found clear labeling of a population of neurons projecting to the bulb which resembled the tubercular-bulbar (TuBu) neurons (Omoto et al., 2017; Figure 5A'), in addition to labeling of the inter-tubercle tract (ITT) (Strausfeld, 1976; Figure 5A''), suggesting inter-hemispheric signaling postsynaptic to MeTu neurons in the AOTU.
evidence: This claim is supported by the trans-Tango labeling shown in Figure 5A'' and inference about function.

claim: R17F12-Gal4 is expressed by a population of two tubercular-tubercle (TuTu) neurons per brain hemisphere.
source: We then identified a Gal4 driver (R17F12-Gal4) that is expressed by a population of two tubercular-tubercle (TuTu) neurons per brain hemisphere, with axonal projections to the contralateral AOTU via the ITT (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical characterization shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TuTu neurons predominantly innervate the intermediate-lateral domain (AOTUil) within the AOTU.
source: Within the AOTU, these TuTu neurons predominantly innervate the intermediate-lateral domain (AOTUil) (Figure 5B').
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 5B'.

claim: TuTuB neurons in the hemibrain connectome are postsynaptic to partially-reconstructed MeTu neurons in the AOTU.
source: The TuTuB neurons are postsynaptic to partially-reconstructed MeTu neurons in the AOTU (MC61), corroborating our trans-Tango results (Figure 5A''), and we suggest that they likely correspond to the TuTu neurons investigated here (see Appendix 1—table 1 for correspondence between neurons in genetic drivers used and neurons in the hemibrain connectome).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the hemibrain connectome data and comparison with the genetic driver expression.

claim: TuTu neurons did not show responses to unpolarized bar stimuli at any of the positions tested.
source: Unexpectedly, we did not find responses to the unpolarized bar stimuli at any of the positions tested (Figure 5C), indicating that these TuTu neurons likely do not mediate the contralateral responses we observed in the MeTu neurons (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the bar response data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TuTu neurons were polarization-sensitive with PSI values similar to those of MeTu neurons.
source: Rather, we found that the TuTu neurons were polarization-sensitive with PSI values similar to those of the MeTu neurons (Figure 5E), and tunings to a limited range of polarization angles (~30°) centered around a near-horizontal orientation (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI analysis shown in Figure 5E and tuning data in Figure 5F.

claim: TuTu neurons showed tunings to a limited range of polarization angles (~30°) centered around a near-horizontal orientation.
source: Rather, we found that the TuTu neurons were polarization-sensitive with PSI values similar to those of the MeTu neurons (Figure 5E), and tunings to a limited range of polarization angles (~30°) centered around a near-horizontal orientation (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning map shown in Figure 5F.

claim: TuBua and TuBus neurons recorded in the AOTU contained high PSI values indicating strong modulation by the polarizer.
source: Among the dendrites of TuBu neurons recorded in the AOTU, we found that the populations innervating the AOTUl and AOTUil domains (TuBus and TuBua, respectively) contained high PSI values that indicated strong modulation by the polarizer (Figure 6B), with average values significantly higher than the background regions of recordings (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI analysis shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: TuBui dendrites innervating the AOTUim domain contained PSI values not greater than 0.5 and were indistinguishable from background regions on average.
source: In contrast, dendrites innervating the AOTUim domain (TuBui) contained PSI values not greater than 0.5 (Figure 6B) and, on average, were indistinguishable from background regions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI analysis shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: TuBua and TuBus dendrites showed a common relationship between preferred angle of polarization and ventral-dorsal position within the AOTU.
source: Pooling data from both domains, the preferred AoP covered a range of angles from −90° to +90° and we found a common relationship between preferred AoP and ventral-dorsal position within the AOTU (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarotopy analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The direction of polarotopy in TuBua and TuBus dendrites matched the direction of polarotopy in the putatively presynaptic MeTu neurons.
source: For the dendrites of TuBua and TuBus neurons, we found that the direction of polarotopy in the AOTU (a counter-clockwise rotation of preferred AoP from ventral to dorsal) matched the direction of polarotopy in the putatively presynaptic MeTu neurons.
evidence: This is a comparison of the polarotopy data from TuBu and MeTu neurons.

claim: The relative positions of tunings along the ventrodorsal axis of the AOTU do not correspond directly between TuBu dendrites and MeTu terminals.
source: However, the relative positions of tunings along the ventrodorsal axis of the AOTU do not correspond directly. For example, in the dorsal half of the AOTU the preferred AoPs of MeTu terminals were in the range 0° to +90° (Figure 3E,F), whereas for TuBua dendrites in the dorsal half of the AOTU preferred AoPs were in the range −90° to 0° (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the tuning ranges in MeTu and TuBu neurons.

claim: The mismatch in tuning positions suggests either inhibitory input from MeTu neurons or integration of additional inputs from unidentified polarization-sensitive elements at TuBu dendrites.
source: If MeTu neurons are indeed presynaptic to TuBu neurons in the AOTU, this result suggests either inhibitory input from MeTu neurons, which would effectively shift the preferred AoP by 90°, or the integration of additional inputs from unidentified polarization-sensitive elements at the dendrites of TuBu neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mismatch in tuning positions between MeTu and TuBu neurons.

claim: The majority of TuBus neurons recorded in micro-glomeruli in the BUs contained low PSI values, with high PSI values interspersed among them.
source: Spatial maps of PSI values revealed that the majority of TuBus neurons recorded in micro-glomeruli in the BUs contained low PSI values, and interspersed among them were micro-glomeruli with high PSI values (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI maps shown in Figure 7A.

claim: All TuBua neurons recorded exhibited high PSI values in the BUa.
source: Finally, we found that all TuBua neurons recorded exhibited high PSI values in the BUa (Figure 7A,B), in two Gal4 drivers.
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Average PSI values in the BUa were greater than 0.5 in both TuBua drivers.
source: Average PSI values in the BUa were greater than 0.5 in both drivers (Figure 7C), while in the BUi and BUs, the average PSI values were not significantly different from the average in background regions of recordings, typically around 0.2 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative PSI analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In the BUi and BUs, average PSI values were not significantly different from the average in background regions of recordings.
source: Average PSI values in the BUa were greater than 0.5 in both drivers (Figure 7C), while in the BUi and BUs, the average PSI values were not significantly different from the average in background regions of recordings, typically around 0.2 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Among active pixels in both the BUs and BUa, there was a significant effect of the polarizer on PSI values versus controls, with the effect size larger in the BUa.
source: Among active pixels in both the BUs and BUa we found a significant effect of the polarizer on PSI values versus controls, with the effect size larger in the latter (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Polarized light responses were found in TuBu neuron output micro-glomeruli in both the superior and anterior bulb.
source: In sum, we found polarized light responses in TuBu neuron output micro-glomeruli in both the superior and anterior bulb, and no appreciable responses to polarized light in TuBu neuron outputs in the inferior bulb.
evidence: This is a summary of the PSI data from the three bulb regions.

claim: No appreciable responses to polarized light were found in TuBu neuron outputs in the inferior bulb.
source: In sum, we found polarized light responses in TuBu neuron output micro-glomeruli in both the superior and anterior bulb, and no appreciable responses to polarized light in TuBu neuron outputs in the inferior bulb.
evidence: This is a summary of the PSI data from the three bulb regions.

claim: A cluster of micro-glomeruli toward the medial edge of the superior bulb tended to show preferential responses to similar angles of polarization.
source: We observed that a cluster of micro-glomeruli toward the medial edge of the superior bulb tended to show preferential responses to similar angles of polarization (AoP) (Figure 7A, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning map shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In the BUs, there was a non-uniform distribution of preferred angles of polarization with the highest frequency around −45° in the left bulb and +45° in the right bulb.
source: When we examined the distribution of preferred AoPs in the BUs we found a non-uniform distribution with the highest frequency of preferred AoPs around −45° in the left bulb (Figure 7F) and +45° in the right bulb (Figure 7F').
evidence: This claim is supported by the polar histograms shown in Figure 7F,F'.

claim: In the anterior bulb (BUa), there was an approximately uniform representation of preferred angles of polarization in TuBua neurons.
source: Conversely, in the anterior bulb (BUa) on both sides we found an approximately uniform representation of preferred AoPs in TuBua neurons (Figure 7G,G').
evidence: This claim is supported by the polar histograms shown in Figure 7G,G'.

claim: Each TuBu neuron connects exclusively with one ring neuron in the bulb.
source: For the neuron populations examined here, our light microscopy images and the hemibrain connectome data (Scheffer et al., 2020) show that each TuBu neuron (BU input) connects exclusively with one ring neuron (BU output), suggesting that the distribution of preferred AoPs in the TuBu populations should be homogeneously sampled by populations of postsynaptic ring neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of light microscopy and hemibrain connectome data.

claim: TuBus and TuBui neuron populations showed responses to unpolarized blue light flash in the AOTU and more strongly in the BU.
source: TuBus and TuBui neuron populations showed responses to the flash in the AOTU and, more strongly, in the BU, while TuBua neurons recorded in either neuropil were inhibited by the unpolarized light stimulus (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flash response data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TuBua neurons were inhibited by unpolarized blue light flash in both the AOTU and BU.
source: TuBus and TuBui neuron populations showed responses to the flash in the AOTU and, more strongly, in the BU, while TuBua neurons recorded in either neuropil were inhibited by the unpolarized light stimulus (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flash response data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ER2 and ER4m ring neuron populations target the outer central domain of the ellipsoid body, albeit following different trajectories.
source: Both ER2 and ER4m ring neuron populations target the outer central domain of the EB, albeit following different trajectories (Figure 8A,B; Omoto et al., 2018; Omoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 8A,B and citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Only a subset of ER2 neurons in the BUs were modulated by polarized light.
source: As with TuBus micro-glomerular outputs, we found that only a subset of ER2 neurons in the BUs were modulated by polarized light, with above-threshold PSI values typically in a medial cluster with a preferred angle of polarization (AoP) around 45° (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI and tuning data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Average PSI values in ER2 neurons were not significantly different from average values in background regions.
source: Low PSI values were common throughout the ER2 population and average values were not significantly different from average values in background regions (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: In ER4m neurons in the BUa, average PSI values were greater than 0.5.
source: By contrast, in ER4m neurons in the BUa, average PSI values were greater than 0.5 (Figure 8D) and the overall distribution of values in the population was similar in shape to the distribution in TuBua neurons (Figure 6B, Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The polarizer had a significant effect on PSI values of ER4m neurons versus controls with the polarizer removed.
source: We found that the polarizer had a significant effect on PSI values of ER4m neurons versus controls with the polarizer removed (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Individual ER4m neurons exhibited distinct preferences for angle of polarization in each recording.
source: Furthermore, we found that the dendrites of individual ER4m neurons exhibited distinct preferences for AoP in each recording (Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning map shown in Figure 8G.

claim: ER4m neurons almost certainly acquire their polarization-tuned responses from the presynaptic TuBua neurons in the BUa.
source: Since ER4m neurons appear to receive monosynaptic input from TuBu neurons, we conclude that they almost certainly acquire their polarization-tuned responses from the presynaptic TuBua neurons in the BUa (Figure 8A,B,F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectivity and response properties of ER4m and TuBua neurons.

claim: The average PSI value decreased from TuBua neurons to ER4m neurons.
source: We note that the average PSI value decreased from TuBua neurons to ER4m neurons (Figure 8G',H', Appendix 1—figure 1B) and we further explore the transformation of their signals in the next section.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of PSI values between TuBua and ER4m neurons.

claim: Modulation of ER4m activity by the polarizer was observed in the ellipsoid body, indicated by their polarization-selectivity index.
source: As expected from recordings in the dendritic regions of ER4m in the anterior bulb (BUa), we observed modulation of their activity with rotations of the polarizer, indicated by their polarization-selectivity index (PSI) (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In some recordings, above-threshold PSI values in ER4m terminals were spatially localized to approximately one quadrant of the ellipsoid body.
source: We noted that in some recordings, above-threshold PSI values were spatially localized to approximately one quadrant of the EB (Figure 9A,B, top, arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI maps shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: Individual ER4m terminals exhibited tunings to distinct angles of polarization, and a range of tunings could be found intermingled at any given position in the ellipsoid body.
source: Individual ER4m terminals exhibited tunings to distinct angles of polarization (AoP), and a range of tunings could be found intermingled at any given position in the EB (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning maps shown in Figure 9B.

claim: In many recordings, the preferred angles of polarization of ER4m terminals were similar to each other and did not represent a full range of angles of polarization.
source: Additionally, we found that in many recordings the preferred angles of polarization (AoPs) of terminals were similar to each other and did not represent a full range of AoPs.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the tuning data across recordings.

claim: The range of angles of polarization found in ER4m terminals varied across animals.
source: The range of AoPs found varied across animals (Figure 9B), and as a result the frequency of preferred AoPs formed a unimodal distribution centered on a different angle in each recording (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning maps and polar histograms shown in Figure 9B,C.

claim: The average activity of an entire ER4m population in the ellipsoid body exhibited modulation induced by the polarizer and a single preferred angle of polarization could be identified for each population.
source: As a result of the non-uniform distributions of preferred AoPs, it followed that the average activity of an entire ER4m population in the EB exhibited modulation induced by the polarizer and a single preferred AoP could effectively be identified for each population (Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the population response data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: For ER4m terminals in the ellipsoid body, population tuning vectors had lengths exceeding 0.74 and an average length of 0.51 across animals.
source: For ER4m terminals in the EB we found population tuning vectors with lengths exceeding 0.74 and an average length of 0.51 across animals (Figure 9E), while for ER4m dendrites recorded in either the left or right BUa individually we found an average length of 0.39 (Figure 9F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the population tuning vector analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claim: For ER4m dendrites recorded in either the left or right BUa individually, the average population tuning vector length was 0.39.
source: For ER4m terminals in the EB we found population tuning vectors with lengths exceeding 0.74 and an average length of 0.51 across animals (Figure 9E), while for ER4m dendrites recorded in either the left or right BUa individually we found an average length of 0.39 (Figure 9F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the population tuning vector analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: For TuBua populations recorded in either bulb, the average population tuning vector length was 0.18 across animals.
source: For TuBua populations recorded in either bulb we found that the vector lengths did not exceed 0.3 and the average length was 0.18 across animals (Figure 9G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the population tuning vector analysis shown in Figure 9G.

claim: The increasing vector length from TuBua to ER4m in the bulb, then from ER4m dendrites in the bulb to terminals in the ellipsoid body, indicates a reduction in the range of angles of polarization found at each stage.
source: This increasing vector length, first from TuBua to ER4m in the bulb, then from the dendrites of ER4m in the bulb to the terminals in the EB, indicates a reduction in the range of AoPs found at each stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the population tuning vector analysis.

claim: There is not an exact correlation between polarized light responses in the populations of presynaptic TuBua neurons and postsynaptic ER4m neurons in an individual animal.
source: These findings suggest that there is not an exact correlation between polarized light responses in the populations of presynaptic TuBua neurons and postsynaptic ER4m neurons in an individual animal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in tuning distributions between TuBua and ER4m neurons.

claim: In ER4m dendrites, the average strength of modulation is reduced compared to TuBua neurons, illustrated by the decrease in PSI values.
source: In ER4m dendrites, the average strength of modulation is reduced compared to TuBua neurons, illustrated by the decrease in PSI values (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Appendix 1—figure 1B), and the distribution of tunings is less uniform (Figure 9F,G).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of PSI values and tuning distributions between TuBua and ER4m neurons.

claim: The ensemble activity of ER4m synapses could convey a preferential response for a particular angle of polarization to columnar neurons at any location in the ellipsoid body.
source: As a consequence, it appears that the ensemble activity of ER4m synapses could convey a preferential response for a particular angle of polarization to columnar neurons at any location in the EB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the population response properties of ER4m neurons.

claim: Ring neurons provide inhibitory input to E-PG neurons in the ellipsoid body.
source: Ring neurons provide inhibitory input to E-PG neurons in the EB (Figure 10A), where interactions between ring and E-PG neurons are thought to be reciprocal (Fisher et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Omoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on ring neuron and E-PG connectivity.

claim: Interactions between ring neurons and E-PG neurons in the ellipsoid body are thought to be reciprocal.
source: Ring neurons provide inhibitory input to E-PG neurons in the EB (Figure 10A), where interactions between ring and E-PG neurons are thought to be reciprocal (Fisher et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Omoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on central complex connectivity.

claim: Connectivity between presynaptic E-PG neurons and postsynaptic ER4m neurons in the ellipsoid body was confirmed using activity-dependent GRASP.
source: We confirmed connectivity between presynaptic E-PG neurons and postsynaptic ER4m neurons in the EB in the genetic drivers used (ER4m: R34D03-LexA, Figure 8B; E-PG: SS00096-Gal4, Figure 10—figure supplement 1A) by labeling synapses using activity-dependent GRASP (Macpherson et al., 2015; Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GRASP data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B.

claim: E-PG activity in the protocerebral bridge was modulated as the angle of polarization rotated.
source: We found that E-PG activity in the PB was indeed modulated as the angle of polarization (AoP) rotated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the calcium imaging data from E-PG neurons.

claim: PSI values and preferred angles of polarization in E-PG neurons showed a bilateral coupling, with the right half of the protocerebral bridge resembling the left half.
source: As expected, the PSI values and preferred AoPs showed a bilateral coupling, with the right half of the PB (1R to 8R) resembling the left half (8L to 1L) (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI and tuning maps shown in Figure 10B,C.

claim: The distribution of PSI values in E-PG neurons was not homogenous across the protocerebral bridge, with high values typically clustering across a contiguous subset of 2–4 glomeruli.
source: We observed that the distribution of PSI values was not homogenous across the PB, and high values typically clustered across a contiguous subset of 2–4 glomeruli, while low PSI values occurred throughout the remaining glomeruli (Figure 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI maps shown in Figure 10B.

claim: In each animal, the preferred angle of polarization was similar across the glomeruli in each cluster of high PSI values.
source: In each animal, the preferred AoP was similar across the glomeruli in each cluster (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning maps shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Overall, substantially lower PSI values were found in E-PG neurons than in ER4m neurons.
source: Overall, we found substantially lower PSI values in E-PG neurons than in ER4m neurons (Figure 10D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI distribution comparison shown in Figure 10D.

claim: A statistically significant effect of the polarizer on PSI values versus controls was found in both E-PG and ER4m populations.
source: We found a statistically significant effect of the polarizer on PSI values versus controls in both populations (Figure 10E), yet the effect size was small in E-PG neurons with an average ΔPSI of 0.06, and an average PSI value that was generally lower than in background regions of recordings (Appendix 1–figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 10E.

claim: The amplitude of responses in E-PG neurons was often found to be inconsistent over multiple rotation cycles of the polarizer.
source: Here, in the PB, we observed characteristics which distinguished E-PG responses from those of all other polarization-sensitive elements that we recorded in the upstream pathway. First, the amplitude of responses was often found to be inconsistent over multiple rotation cycles of the polarizer (arrowhead, Figure 10F, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by the time-series data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: The peak response in E-PG neurons was often found to occur at different positions of the polarizer over multiple cycles.
source: Second, the peak response was often found to occur at different positions of the polarizer over multiple cycles (Figure 10F, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by the time-series data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: Variations in response amplitude and peak position were synchronized across the left and right protocerebral bridge glomerulus pair.
source: For both of these response characteristics, variations were synchronized across the left and right PB glomerulus pair (Figure 10F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the paired glomerulus response data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: PSI values and preferred angles of polarization in E-PG neurons varied over time when analyzed for individual cycles of the polarizer.
source: When we analyzed responses to individual cycles of the polarizer separately, these characteristics manifested as PSI values and preferred AoPs which varied over time (Figure 10G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cycle-by-cycle analysis shown in Figure 10G.

claim: Less than half of all E-PG glomeruli recorded exhibited a periodicity that matched the stimulus.
source: For E-PG neurons, we found that less than half of all glomeruli recorded exhibited a periodicity which matched the stimulus, while almost all ER4m and TuBua neurons matched the stimulus (E-PG: 43.3%, ER4m: 98.4%, TuBua: 100%) (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the auto-correlation analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Almost all ER4m and TuBua neurons exhibited a periodicity that matched the stimulus.
source: For E-PG neurons, we found that less than half of all glomeruli recorded exhibited a periodicity which matched the stimulus, while almost all ER4m and TuBua neurons matched the stimulus (E-PG: 43.3%, ER4m: 98.4%, TuBua: 100%) (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the auto-correlation analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Across different animals, glomeruli at corresponding positions in the protocerebral bridge exhibited different preferred angles of polarization.
source: Across different animals, glomeruli at corresponding positions in the PB exhibited different preferred angles of polarization (AoPs) (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning maps from different animals shown in Figure 10C.

claim: There was no common relationship between glomerulus position in the protocerebral bridge and the preferred angles of polarization of E-PG neurons across animals.
source: Across animals, we again found no common relationship between glomerulus position in the PB and the preferred AoPs of E-PG neurons (Figure 10H), matching the findings for the homologous CL1a neurons in locusts (Heinze and Homberg, 2009; Pegel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 10H and citations to locust studies.

claim: Glomeruli neighboring the glomerulus with the highest PSI value (G0) at ±1 protocerebral bridge position were likely to exhibit a similar preferred angle of polarization to G0, to within 15°.
source: More generally, we found that glomeruli neighboring G0, at ±1 PB position, were likely to exhibit a similar preferred AoP to G0, to within 15° (Figure 10I, Figure 10—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning shift analysis shown in Figure 10I.

claim: At ±2–4 protocerebral bridge positions from G0, preferred angles of polarization generally shifted toward orthogonal angles.
source: At ±2–4 PB positions from G0, we found preferred AoPs generally shifted toward orthogonal angles (Figure 10I, Figure 10—figure supplement 1F,G) and among these positions there was again a similarity between neighboring glomeruli (Figure 10—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning shift analysis shown in Figure 10I and supplementary figures.

claim: The encoding of polarization information in E-PG neurons could be viewed as a limited representation of two approximately orthogonal angles of polarization.
source: Simplistically, this could be viewed as a limited representation of two approximately orthogonal angles of polarization among E-PG neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the tuning data from E-PG neurons.

claim: Each section of the Drosophila anterior visual pathway contains polarization-tuned neurons.
source: In this study, we have demonstrated that each section of the Drosophila anterior visual pathway (AVP) contains polarization-tuned neurons.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The anterior visual pathway neurons provide a circuit to convey polarized light signals from the dorsal rim area of the eye to the compass neurons of the central complex, via the anterior optic tubercle and bulb.
source: Together, they provide a circuit to convey polarized light signals from the specialized dorsal rim area of the eye to the compass neurons of the central complex, via the anterior optic tubercle and bulb.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the connectivity and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The anterior visual pathway also conveys information about unpolarized visual features.
source: This pathway also conveys information about unpolarized visual features, as shown here and in previous studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bar and optic-flow response data in the current study and citations to previous studies.

claim: The encoding of multiple visual modalities, similarities in constituent neurons, and organization of neuropils support the view that the anterior visual pathway in Drosophila is homologous to the sky compass pathway described in other insects.
source: The encoding of multiple visual modalities, the similarities in the constituent neurons, and the organization of the neuropils which accommodate them (Omoto et al., 2017), support the view that the AVP in Drosophila is homologous to the sky compass pathway described in locusts, bees, butterflies, and beetles, among other insects (Honkanen et al., 2019; Warren et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the current findings and comparison with other insects, supported by citations.

claim: Almost the full extent of the dorsal rim area was stimulated by polarized light originating from a single point in the visual field with a common angle of polarization.
source: Surprisingly, almost the full extent of the DRA was stimulated by polarized light originating from a single point in the visual field with a common angle of polarization.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that a wide range of polarization tunings was revealed in downstream neurons despite the stimulus configuration.

claim: The Drosophila medulla dorsal rim area analyzes the overall pattern of polarized light in the sky and extracts a predominant angle of polarization.
source: A wide range of polarization tunings was subsequently revealed in downstream neurons, supporting the idea that the Drosophila medulla dorsal rim area (MEDRA) analyzes the overall pattern of polarized light in the sky and extracts a predominant angle of polarization (AoP) (Labhart, 2016; Rossel and Wehner, 1986), rather than performing many local AoP estimates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the response properties of downstream neurons and citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: During the morning and evening when D. melanogaster are most active, the pattern of polarization in the sky can be well approximated by a single, predominant angle of polarization.
source: During the morning and evening when D. melanogaster are most active, the pattern of polarization in the sky can be well approximated by a single, predominant AoP.
evidence: This is a statement about the natural polarization patterns during Drosophila activity periods, based on knowledge of atmospheric optics.

claim: DmDRA1 neurons spatially integrate polarization signals from multiple columns of the MEDRA.
source: DmDRA1 neurons appear to spatially integrate polarization signals from multiple columns of the MEDRA (Figure 1), and individual neurons heavily overlap each other (Sancer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on the anatomical properties of DmDRA1 neurons and their response properties.

claim: Spatial integration by DmDRA1 neurons could provide robustness to occlusions of the sky or of the dorsal rim area itself and average out inconsistencies in the available light.
source: This could provide an additional robustness to occlusions of the sky or of the DRA itself and average out inconsistencies in the available light (Labhart et al., 2001; Rossel and Wehner, 1986).
evidence: This is an inference about the functional benefit of spatial integration, supported by citations.

claim: The parallel circuitry between DRA R7, DmDRA1, and MeTu neurons in MEDRA columns resembles the color-processing pathway found in non-DRA columns involving R7, Dm8, and Tm5c.
source: The parallel circuitry between DRA R7, DmDRA1, and MeTu neurons in MEDRA columns (Figure 2D), resembles the color-processing pathway found in non-DRA columns involving R7, Dm8, and Tm5c (Gao et al., 2008; Karuppudurai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of circuit motifs based on anatomical and functional similarities, supported by citations.

claim: Color and polarization processing are compatible in MeTu neurons.
source: MeTu neurons in the MEDRA may also integrate color signals, as their dendritic fields extend into the non-DRA medulla, indicating that color and polarization processing are compatible (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical properties of MeTu neurons.

claim: The AOTU in Drosophila is likely to be a site for modulation of signals depending on time or internal states.
source: The AOTU in Drosophila is also likely to be a site for modulation of signals depending on time or internal states (el Jundi et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2018; Lamaze et al., 2018), and a capacity to modify responses may explain why we observed multiple polarotopic organizations in a MeTu neuron population in the AOTU (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to previous research and the observation of variable polarotopy.

claim: TuBu neurons extract a processed form of the signals in the AOTU, encoding visual features within fewer neurons than the MeTu populations.
source: Our findings suggest that TuBu neurons extract a processed form of the signals in the AOTU, encoding visual features within fewer neurons than the MeTu populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of tuning properties and neuron numbers between MeTu and TuBu populations.

claim: TuBu neurons appear to divide signals into functional groups.
source: TuBu neurons appear to divide signals into functional groups, and the anterior bulb-projecting TuBua group in every fly contained a set of around six tunings covering −90° to +90° of polarization space in approximately 30° steps, tightly packed in a micro-glomerular structure with no apparent polarotopy (Figure 7, Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of tuning distributions in TuBua neurons.

claim: The site of integration of celestial cues is not at the synapse between TuBu and ring neurons.
source: Hence, we posit that the site of integration of celestial cues is not at the synapse between TuBu and ring neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the one-to-one connectivity between TuBu and ring neurons.

claim: The populations of TuBus neurons recorded contained a limited range of tunings and resembled a system for detecting visual features with a particular polarization signature.
source: Although we found evidence that angles of polarization are represented in the superior bulb (Figure 7, Figure 8), where unpolarized cues are also known to be represented, the populations we recorded contained a limited range of tunings and resembled a system for detecting visual features with a particular polarization signature (Labhart, 2016), such as horizontally polarized light reflected from surfaces like water, rather than a system for accurate estimation of orientation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the tuning distributions in TuBus neurons, supported by a citation.

claim: ER4m ring neurons do not simply relay the responses of presynaptic TuBua neurons to the ellipsoid body.
source: By recording the ensemble response of a population of ER4m ring neurons, both in the anterior bulb and ellipsoid body (EB), we determined that they do not simply relay the responses of presynaptic TuBua neurons to the EB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in response properties between TuBua and ER4m neurons.

claim: ER4m ring neurons appear to deliver a subset of signals more prominently than others, bestowing the population with an ensemble response tuned to a specific angle of polarization.
source: Instead, they appear to deliver a subset of signals more prominently than others, bestowing the population with an ensemble response tuned to a specific angle of polarization (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is based on the population tuning analysis of ER4m neurons.

claim: The population tuning of ER4m neurons conveys a different angle of polarization in individual animals.
source: Furthermore, we found that this population tuning conveys a different angle of polarization in individual animals, and one exciting possibility is that this represents a flexible heading signal relative to polarized light cues, which could direct behavior (Warren et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on the variability of population tunings across animals and speculation about functional significance.

claim: Among ER4m and E-PG neurons, polarization tunings are not represented with a retinotopic map in the ellipsoid body or protocerebral bridge which is common between individual animals.
source: It is clear that among ER4m and E-PG neurons, polarization tunings are not represented with a retinotopic map in the EB or PB which is common between individual animals (Figure 9, Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of tuning organizations across animals.

claim: The lack of organization in E-PG responses matches previous findings that the azimuthal position of unpolarized visual stimuli is not represented retinotopically in E-PG neurons.
source: This is in contrast with the consistent polarotopic organizations found upstream in the MEDRA or AOTU (Figures 1–6), but in agreement with a previous study which showed that the azimuthal position of unpolarized visual stimuli is also not represented retinotopically in E-PG neurons (Fisher et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: The lack of organization in E-PG responses matches previous findings in the corresponding CL1a neurons in locusts.
source: The lack of organization in E-PG responses also matches previous findings in the corresponding CL1a neurons in locusts, but contrasts with the polarotopic organization found in other columnar neurons in the locust CX, such as CPU1, and the tangential TB1 neurons (Heinze and Homberg, 2009; Heinze and Homberg, 2007; Pegel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous studies in locusts, supported by citations.

claim: E-PG neurons may respond to one of two approximately orthogonal angles of polarization, effectively dividing the population into two groups.
source: Our data suggest that in a given fly, E-PG neurons may respond to one of two approximately orthogonal angles of polarization, effectively dividing the population into two groups.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the tuning data from E-PG neurons.

claim: A binary system of two orthogonal preferred angles would be well suited to influence downstream processes in a motor-centered coordinate frame.
source: A binary system such as this would be well suited to influence downstream processes in a motor-centered coordinate frame (Rayshubskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the binary tuning system, supported by a citation.

claim: The eventual output of the compass network may be a command signal to activate one descending neuron of a bilateral pair to initiate a turn to either the left or right.
source: For example, the eventual output of the compass network may be a command signal to activate one descending neuron of a bilateral pair to initiate a turn to either the left or right, and thus maintain a heading specified by polarization patterns in the sky.
evidence: This is speculation about how the polarization signals might influence motor output.

claim: An activity bump was not observed in E-PG neurons in the protocerebral bridge, likely due to the open-loop stimulus presentation and recordings performed in immobilized animals.
source: We did not observe an activity bump in E-PG neurons in the PB, likely due to the open-loop stimulus presentation and recordings performed in immobilized animals, although we could see evidence of flexible encoding of polarization information (Figure 10).
evidence: This is an inference about why the activity bump was not observed, based on experimental conditions.

claim: In behavioral studies in ants and dung beetles, skylight polarization cues have been demonstrated to have a greater influence than other visual features in guidance and navigation behaviors.
source: Behavioral studies in ants (Wehner and Müller, 2006) and dung beetles (el Jundi et al., 2015) have demonstrated that skylight polarization cues can have a greater influence than other visual features in guidance and navigation behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies in other insects.

claim: In Drosophila, intensity gradients have been shown to have a greater behavioral significance than polarized light.
source: In Drosophila, intensity gradients have been shown to have a greater behavioral significance than polarized light (Warren et al., 2018), yet recent connectome analysis of the Drosophila CX highlights the polarization-sensitive ring neurons that we identified here as potentially being at the top of a hierarchy of sensory inputs (Hulse et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to a behavioral study and a connectome analysis.

claim: Recent connectome analysis of the Drosophila central complex highlights the polarization-sensitive ring neurons as potentially being at the top of a hierarchy of sensory inputs.
source: In Drosophila, intensity gradients have been shown to have a greater behavioral significance than polarized light (Warren et al., 2018), yet recent connectome analysis of the Drosophila CX highlights the polarization-sensitive ring neurons that we identified here as potentially being at the top of a hierarchy of sensory inputs (Hulse et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a connectome analysis.
